title: Since 1946 the US president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterm elections
body: On 3 November 2026 Americans elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 senators, halfway through a presidential term. In every midterm since 1946 except two, 1998 and 2002, the president’s party lost House seats: about 26 on average, and 63 in 2010. In the Senate it lost seats in 13 of those 20 midterms. Midterms are widely read as a referendum on the president, who is not on the ballot. Senators serve six-year terms in three staggered classes, so only about a third of the Senate is elected at once: in 2026 the 33 seats of one class, plus special elections in Ohio and Florida for seats left empty when their senators joined the new administration.

slides.question: Of the 20 US midterm elections from 1946 to 2022, in how many did the president’s party lose House seats?
slides.explanation: 18 of 20. The only gains were in 1998, under Bill Clinton (+4), and 2002, under George W. Bush (+8).

slides.alt: Animation on ballot paper: the US Capitol and 435 House seats. Twenty bars show the House seats won or lost by the president's party in each midterm since 1946, nearly all losses; 1998 and 2002 stand out. A ballot card, then the Senate's 100 seats in three classes, 35 of them up in 2026.

slides.prompt: Tap through every midterm since 1946. Find the two in which the president’s party gained House seats.
slides.takeaway: 1998, under Clinton, and 2002, under George W. Bush. In every other midterm since 1946 the president’s party lost House seats: 18 of 20. Switch to the Senate: there it lost in 13.

slides.heading: House seats lost by the president’s party, recent midterms
slides.note: American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara

slides.heading: Why only a third of the Senate
slides.text: The Constitution gives senators six-year terms and splits them into three classes, so one class is elected every two years. The whole House, with two-year terms, is elected every time. That is why the House can swing much further in a single election.

slides.question: When did the president’s party last gain House seats in a midterm?
slides.explanation: In 2002, a year after the 11 September attacks, George W. Bush’s Republicans gained 8 House seats and 2 Senate seats. Every midterm since has cost the president’s party House seats.
